title: The Case of the Missing Biscuit Label
markdown:
Coach Fern, bless her organized heart, had a vision of cupboards so tidy you could hear a pin drop. In this scout hut, of course, that pin had probably been borrowed by a goat.

The Miscellaneous Cupboard was her battlefield: forgotten camping gear, leftover craft supplies, and the occasional runaway sock. It showed how gifted the Hemlock Hollow Scouts were at leaving things in odd spots.

"Right, troop!" Her voice was as chirpy as a robin at breakfast. Sensible tweed, hands on hips. "Today we bring order. Today we label!"

Arlo the goat arrived in his usual capacity, which was not tidying. He was trying to balance a scout handbook on his horns. The pages fluttered like confused birds. His eyes had already found things worth nibbling. Beside him, Cleo the cat watched with her bored expression, tail on a slow thoughtful swish, as if to say this might be slightly interesting.

Coach Fern's prize was a shiny new label maker. She was not merely naming shelves. She was writing little lives for each object. Crumpled tin foil became: "Glimmering Wrapper, holder of campfire stories and accidental bird feeders." The old skipping rope: "Springy String, once used in a legendary double-dutch that ended in a spectacular tie and three very dizzy scouts."

The scouts, startled at first, got hooked. They lingered, reading, laughing at jokes that were almost too accurate. Someone had labeled a lantern for lighting dark evenings and finding lost beetles. Someone else had given the tent pegs credit for artistic leaning.

Young Pipkin frowned at a rusty compass. "Once pointed North, then South, then towards Mrs. Higgins' prize-winning petunias. Its sense of direction is… creative." Giggles traveled the hut. Even Cleo flicked an ear, which from Cleo counted as a standing ovation.

In the new-scouts corner, a shy girl named Lily held a well-loved book to her chest and read every label twice, as if the cupboard were a library that had finally noticed her. She had only joined last week.

Arlo was more interested in the labels' papery crunch. He proved this on "Sticky Tape, guardian of torn maps and surprise bandages."

Cleo nudged him, a purr of disapproval. "Uncouth. And you a creature who claims to appreciate a dandelion stem."

The true jewel was the Emergency Biscuit Tin — Coach Fern's reserve for scout-related sadness: maps dissolved in rain, mud that had learned to cling to ceilings. Its label was a work of art.

"The Last Hope Tin: Holds food for tired souls and a sprinkle of never-give-up hope. Do Not Open, unless you've lost all hope (and maybe your snacks)."

Coach Fern said it was the most important thing in the hut, after the first-aid kit and her secret spare shoelaces.

One windy Tuesday, while the troop wrestled new knots, a shared gasp went through the room. The tin sat on its shelf. The label was gone. The tin looked bare, like a king without a crown. The wind sighed through a gap in the window.

"My label!" Coach Fern's organized world crumbled like a stale biscuit. "The heart of the cupboard! Did it wander off? Run away with the spare batteries?"

Arlo, who had been nervously chewing his tail, looked up and nudged Cleo. "Something's missing."

"Indeed. And knowing you, I would suspect that hole you call a home. This time it smells of worry, not just damp hay."

A search party formed. The scouts put down their knots with a sense of duty that would have pleased Coach Fern on a tidier day. Arlo sniffed like a detective. "Biscuit. Paper-y biscuit. And something shy. Like a mouse at a party."

Cleo scanned the ceiling beams. "Nothing up here. Though a dusty spider is having a long think about cobwebs. He looks quite philosophical. I wouldn't ask him about biscuits."

They hunted the whole hut. The Sparkling Lantern, for lighting dark evenings and finding lost beetles, offered no hints. The Wobbly Tent Pegs, experts at leaning in funny ways, were no help at all. Coach Fern eyed the spare biscuit tin as if it might have eloped with the shoelaces.

Arlo stopped again at the new-scouts corner and pointed his nose at Lily's book. Tucked between the pages, kept as if it were a pressed flower, was the missing label. Lily's cheeks went raspberry. She held the book tighter.

"I borrowed it," she whispered, dry leaves of a voice. "The stories on the labels… I wanted to read about the biscuits. I felt a bit lost. The label made the tin look important. I thought if something so important had a story, maybe I would have a story here too."

The wind seemed to pause. Coach Fern's stern face softened. She knelt, tweed rustling.

"Oh, my dear. You didn't need to borrow the label to find a story here. You're in it. Every scout brings a chapter. Even the ones who have only just opened the book."

She lifted the label, smooth and cool. Arlo, guilty for his suspicions, nudged Lily's hand — gentle, for a goat. Cleo, for once not distant, offered a rumbling purr.

The label went home. The Last Hope Tin looked like itself again. The scouts returned to their knots with less drama than they had brought to the search, which Coach Fern counted as progress.

Arlo decided paper was best left to labels, and that his own stories were better told in bleats and the occasional friendly head-butt. Coach Fern glanced at Lily, already reading the compass again, and made a private note to print a second copy of the biscuit label — not as a spare for the cupboard, but as a page a new scout might keep without emptying the shelf.
